items.title: Scientists Build 6,986 Digital Brain Twins to Study Dementia
items.snippet: Every human brain ages within a unique biological and social context. An international team created 6,986 personalized biophysical "digital brain twins" across 16 countries, turning fMRI scans into virtual laboratories to decode how aging, dementia, and environmental exposures alter neural dynamics.

items.title: High-Speed Nanoscale Brain Imaging Uncovers Hidden Synapses
items.snippet: Even the most detailed brain wiring maps often miss ultra-fine cellular connections. Researchers sped up 3D electron tomography 50-fold, uncovering hidden electrical synapses and tiny protrusions where neurons appear to "nibble" neighboring glia.

items.title: Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?
items.snippet: Parents and teachers often tell kids that studying harder will make learning enjoyable, but psychology research suggests the opposite. A new study shows that effort boosts understanding, while genuine interest must come first to spark engagement.

items.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.snippet: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. items.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.snippet: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

items.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.snippet: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities.
